client: I've been really struggling since my dad passed away two months ago. Every time I go to a family gathering, it just hits me all over again — like this wave of sadness I can't control, and I end up feeling worse than if I'd just stayed home. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I should at least try.
therapist: Thank you for being here and for giving this a try, even when part of you isn't sure it will help — that takes real courage, especially when you're carrying something this heavy. I notice that as you're describing all of this, there's a quietness in how you're speaking, almost like the weight of it goes even deeper than the words themselves. I'm wondering — beneath the sadness you mentioned, is there something else sitting with you that's harder to name?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, I think there is something harder to name. It's like... underneath the sadness there's this constant hum of guilt, like I should have done more to keep the friendships I've lost, and I didn't, and now I'm just sitting with that. It's embarrassing to even say out loud because part of me thinks I brought the loneliness on myself.
therapist: It means a lot that you said that out loud — guilt has a way of hiding in the shadows and growing heavier the longer it stays unnamed. I want to gently offer a thought: the fact that you're grieving these friendships actually shows how much they mattered to you, and that's not the same thing as having caused the loss. What does that inner voice sound like when it tells you that you "brought this on yourself" — is it harsh, or more like a quiet, persistent whisper?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: It's more like a quiet, persistent whisper, honestly — it doesn't scream at me, it just kind of... lingers there in the background, like a low hum I can't turn off. It says things like "you were too much," or "you should have tried harder to keep in touch," and it feels so matter-of-fact, like it's just stating obvious truths rather than being cruel. I guess that's what makes it hard to push back against — it doesn't feel like an attack, it feels like a verdict.
therapist: That image of a "verdict" is so telling — verdicts feel final, authoritative, like they've already been decided, which makes them so much harder to challenge than an obvious attack. In CBT, we'd call that voice a cognitive distortion, but what strikes me is that even as you're describing it so calmly, there's a heaviness underneath that feels like it costs you something just to carry it around all day. I'm curious — if a close friend came to you and said "I think I was too much for the people I've lost," what would you actually say back to them?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I'd probably tell them that's not true, that they weren't too much, that the people who left just weren't the right fit. But when I try to turn that around on myself, it just... doesn't land the same way. It feels like I'm allowed to be generous with other people but when it comes to me, there's this wall that goes up and the kindness just bounces off.
therapist: What you just described — that wall where kindness bounces off — is one of the most honest things a person can recognize about themselves, and it tells me the compassion is actually *there*, it's just not yet finding a way through to you. It's almost like you have two sets of rules: a generous one for everyone else, and a much harsher standard that only applies to you, and somewhere along the way that felt like the *safe* or *right* way to be. I'm wondering — do you have any sense of when you first learned that you didn't deserve the same kindness you give to others?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think... it goes back pretty far, honestly. I remember being maybe ten or eleven and my mom was going through a really hard time, and I learned pretty quickly that my feelings were kind of an inconvenience, that the way to be "good" was to not need things. It wasn't like anyone said that out loud, but I just absorbed it somehow, and I guess I never really unlearned it.
therapist: What you just uncovered is really significant — as a child, you did something incredibly adaptive to survive a hard situation, you made yourself small and needless, but that survival strategy has followed you all the way into adulthood and is now the very wall that keeps kindness out. There's something tender in the way you're speaking about that little ten-year-old version of you, almost carefully, like you're handling something fragile. I want to ask — when you think about that child who learned to stop needing things, what do you feel toward them?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I feel... sad, I think. Like, genuinely sad in a way that surprised me just now when you said that. It's like I want to tell that kid that they didn't have to do that, that it wasn't their fault things were so hard, but then I also feel this weird guilt, like I'm being dramatic or self-indulgent by even feeling sorry for myself.
therapist: That sadness you just felt — the kind that surprised you — that's actually something really important, because it means a part of you is ready to be seen. I notice you're speaking quite softly right now, almost carefully, like you're holding something very delicate, and I wonder if underneath the sadness there's also something that feels a little fragile or even frightening about letting yourself grieve for that child. The fact that you immediately called it "dramatic" is that same old wall appearing right on cue — but what if feeling sad for a ten-year-old who had to stop needing things is actually one of the most reasonable responses there is?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to agree with it... but there's also this voice in my head that says if I start feeling sorry for that kid, I'll just fall apart completely and never pull myself back together. Like, what's the point of grieving something that happened twenty years ago when I still have to get up and function tomorrow? I guess that's the frightening part — not the sadness itself, but what happens if I let it actually land.
therapist: That fear of falling apart and never coming back together is one of the most common things that keeps people from grieving — but here's what I've seen to be true: the falling apart you're afraid of is actually far less dangerous than the weight of carrying it sealed up forever. What strikes me is that you've already let some of this land just now, in this conversation, and you're still here, still thinking clearly, still putting words to it — which suggests you might be more resilient than that frightened part of you believes. I'm wondering if the grief isn't actually the threat, but rather the thing that might finally start to loosen that wall a little.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it... but another part of me is like, okay, this is just a conversation, it's contained, there are rules here. Out there in my actual life, if I start to crack open, there's no one sitting across from me making sure I'm okay. That's what scares me — not the grief itself maybe, but doing it completely alone.
therapist: What you just named is so real and so important — the fear isn't about the grief itself, it's about facing it without a net, without someone there to witness it with you. And there's something that strikes me in how you said that, a kind of urgency, like this loneliness isn't just about the past but is something you're feeling very much right now, in the present. I want to sit with that for a moment — because part of what we might explore together is what it would look like to slowly, carefully build that sense of support in your life, so that grief doesn't have to mean being completely alone with it.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, you're right that it's very present for me right now, not just some old wound I'm picking at. But when you say "build support" — I don't even know where to start with that, because honestly most of the people in my life don't really get what I'm going through, and trying to explain it feels exhausting before I've even begun. It's like the effort of reaching out almost makes the loneliness worse, if that makes any sense.
therapist: That makes complete sense — sometimes the anticipation of not being understood is its own kind of exhaustion, and it can feel safer to stay silent than to reach out and have it fall flat. But I'm noticing something as you're saying this — your words are describing feeling stuck and tired, yet there's an energy in your voice right now, almost like something quickened, like a part of you is more alive to this topic than the words alone are letting on. I'm curious — underneath the exhaustion of explaining yourself, is there also a part of you that actually *wants* to be known by someone, maybe even quite urgently?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Yeah... I mean, of course there's a part of me that wants that. I'm not going to pretend that's not true. But wanting it and actually believing it's possible are two really different things, and most of the time the second one just isn't there for me.
therapist: The honesty in that is striking — you're not pretending, you're just telling the truth about where you are, and that gap between wanting connection and believing it's possible is such a painful place to live. The way you said that just now was very quiet, almost like something deflated a little, like even naming the want out loud cost you something. I wonder if that belief — that connection isn't really possible for you — is something that was handed to you a long time ago by that same little kid who learned not to need things, rather than something you've actually had the chance to test on your own terms.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech
